lead: A semiconductor laser diode is a forward-biased p-n junction that supplies its own light and its own mirrors. Cleaved crystal faces at the two ends form a Fabry–Perot cavity. Below a threshold current the diode behaves like an expensive LED; above it, stimulated emission wins and the output becomes narrow-band, directional and coherent. Every long-haul link, metro ring and FTTH feeder in India starts from one of these devices. Some syllabi call it an injection laser diode (ILD).
prereq: You need: 3.1 for stimulated emission, 3.2 for the forward-biased emitting junction, and 3.3 for population inversion, feedback and the threshold gain condition.

sections.h3: The diode is its own cavity

blocks.text: A laser diode is a p-n junction with a very thin active layer — tens of nanometres to about 0.1 µm — between two wider-bandgap cladding layers. Forward bias injects electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side into that layer, and they recombine there. At low current the device emits spontaneous light exactly as the LED of 3.2 does.

Two things change the picture. The active layer is thin and the current density high, so carriers are injected faster than spontaneous recombination alone can remove them. The carrier density builds until the recombination rate matches the injection rate, and at that density population inversion exists between the bands — the condition from 3.3. And the crystal is cleaved along natural planes at both ends, leaving two flat parallel faces. The semiconductor index is near 3.5 and air is 1, so each face reflects a fraction R = ((n − 1)/(n + 1))² ≈ 0.30, where n is the refractive index.

Thirty per cent per facet is enough. Light travelling along the cavity is amplified by stimulated emission on each pass, reflects at a facet and comes back. Gain per pass must exceed loss per pass — mirror loss plus internal loss — and that is the threshold of 3.3.

sections.h3: Threshold, slope efficiency and the L-I curve

blocks.text: Written as a current density, the threshold condition in the linear-gain approximation is:

J<sub>th</sub> is threshold current density in A/m² (device data sheets quote A/cm²); α<sub>i</sub> is internal loss per metre; α<sub>m</sub> = (1/2L)·ln(1/(R₁R₂)) is mirror loss per metre for cavity length L in metres and facet reflectivities R₁, R₂; Γ is the confinement factor, the fraction of the optical mode overlapping the active layer; β is gain per metre per A/m².

A double heterostructure confines both carriers and the optical field to the thin active layer. The carrier confinement raises the gain coefficient β and the heterobarriers keep αi small, so Jth falls even though Γ is only a few tenths (typically 0.1–0.4 for a bulk active layer). Quantum wells go further (see 3.5).

A shorter cavity raises α<sub>m</sub> and so raises J<sub>th</sub>, but the active area shrinks, so the threshold current I<sub>th</sub> = J<sub>th</sub> × area falls. Lengthening the cavity lowers α<sub>m</sub> and J<sub>th</sub>, but raises I<sub>th</sub>. Cavity length trades threshold current against mirror loss.
Above threshold the light-current curve is a straight line:

blocks.where: P is emitted optical power in W; I is forward current in A; I<sub>th</sub> is threshold current in A; η<sub>s</sub> is slope efficiency in W/A, and η<sub>s</sub> = η<sub>d</sub> (hν/q) with η<sub>d</sub> the differential quantum efficiency (a pure number, at most 1), hν the photon energy in J and q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

blocks.text: Typical values for a Fabry–Perot laser at 1.3–1.55 µm are I<sub>th</sub> = 10–30 mA and η<sub>s</sub> = 0.1–0.3 W/A. Subtract I<sub>th</sub>, never I. Below threshold the curve in the figure sits almost on the axis: the diode gives only a weak spontaneous tail of a few microwatts.
The cavity is a few hundred micrometres long, so many longitudinal modes fit inside the gain band. Their spacing is:

blocks.where: Δλ is mode spacing in m; λ is centre wavelength in m; n<sub>g</sub> is group index, about 3.5–4; L is cavity length in m. For λ = 1.55 µm, n<sub>g</sub> = 3.5, L = 300 µm, Δλ ≈ 1.14 nm.

blocks.text: Transverse modes are set by waveguide width and layer structure. A ridge a few micrometres wide supports one transverse mode, which is what a single-mode fiber needs; a broad stripe oscillates in several and is harder to couple (see 3.6).

T and T₀ are temperatures in kelvin and T<sub>c</sub> is the characteristic temperature in kelvin. T<sub>c</sub> is 50–70 K for InGaAsP devices near 1.3 µm and above 100 K for GaAs-based ones; a small T<sub>c</sub> means the laser needs a cooler or a bias-tracking circuit.

Direct modulation adds the signal to the bias current. The diode must stay biased above threshold, otherwise every pulse starts with a turn-on delay. Carrier density and refractive index move together, so the wavelength chirps during each pulse, and that chirp turns into dispersion penalty in the fiber (see chromatic dispersion, with fiber signal degradation). Directly modulated DFB lasers serve short and metro links at up to about 10 Gb/s; for longer reach or higher rates an external modulator is used (see 3.8).

figure.caption: Output power against current for the worked example’s laser: almost nothing below the 20 mA threshold, then a straight line of slope 0.30 W/A, so 40 mA gives 6.0 mW and 60 mA gives 12.0 mW. Always subtract the threshold before multiplying by the slope.

spec.aria: A light-current plot from 0 to 70 milliamps and 0 to 15 milliwatts. The output stays near zero up to 20 milliamps, then rises in a straight line. Points at 40 milliamps, 6 milliwatts and 60 milliamps, 12 milliwatts, with a slope triangle of 6 milliwatts over 20 milliamps, 0.30 watts per amp. A note gives the differential quantum efficiency 0.317 at 1.31 micrometres.

examples.question: A Fabry–Perot laser diode has threshold current 20 mA and slope efficiency 0.30 W/A. (a) Find the output optical power at 40 mA and at 60 mA. (b) At 60 mA the forward voltage is 1.8 V; find the electrical input power and the overall efficiency. (c) The laser emits at 1.31 µm; find its differential quantum efficiency η<sub>d</sub>.
steps: Convert currents to amperes: I<sub>th</sub> = 0.020 A, 40 mA = 0.040 A, 60 mA = 0.060 A.
Electrical input at 60 mA: P<sub>elec</sub> = V·I = 1.8 × 0.060 = 0.108 W = 108 mW.
Overall efficiency: η = 12.0 mW / 108 mW = 0.111, i.e. 11.1%. Most of the input is heat, which is why a laser package sits on a heat sink.
Photon energy in volts: hν/q = 1.24/1.31 = 0.947 V. Then η<sub>d</sub> = η<sub>s</sub>/(hν/q) = 0.30/0.947 = 0.317: about 32% of the extra electrons above threshold give an output photon.
examples.answer: 6.0 mW at 40 mA and 12.0 mW at 60 mA; at 60 mA the input is 108 mW and the overall efficiency is 11.1%. The differential quantum efficiency is 0.317.

traps: Using the whole current instead of (I − I<sub>th</sub>): at 60 mA with η<sub>s</sub> = 0.30 W/A you get 18 mW, not 12 mW.
Slope efficiency is a slope in W/A, not a percentage. The percentage is the differential quantum efficiency η<sub>d</sub>, and the two differ by the factor hν/q.
Threshold current (mA) and threshold current density (A/cm²) are different quantities; J<sub>th</sub> multiplied by active area gives I<sub>th</sub>.
Longitudinal mode spacing comes from cavity length, transverse modes come from waveguide width. Examiners swap the two words.
Mirror loss α<sub>m</sub> and internal loss α<sub>i</sub> are separate terms that add inside J<sub>th</sub>; a small R lowers reflectivity and raises threshold, it does not raise output.

quiz.q: Define slope efficiency and give its unit.
quiz.a: Slope efficiency η<sub>s</sub> is the increase in output optical power per unit increase in current above threshold. Unit: W/A.

quiz.q: What fraction of light is reflected at an uncoated cleaved facet of a laser with n = 3.5?
Why does the L-I curve not rise from I = 0?
quiz.a: Below threshold the gain per pass is less than mirror plus internal loss, so stimulated emission cannot build up. Only spontaneous emission escapes, a few microwatts growing weakly with current. Above I<sub>th</sub> the gain clamps at the loss value and extra current converts to coherent output.

quiz.q: Why does a double heterostructure lower the threshold current density?
quiz.a: It confines both carriers and the optical mode to a thin active layer. Carrier confinement greatly increases the gain β per unit current density and keeps the internal loss α<sub>i</sub> small; Γ is only moderate (a few tenths) but the product Γβ still rises, so J<sub>th</sub> = (α<sub>i</sub> + α<sub>m</sub>)/(Γβ) drops. The thin layer also shrinks the active volume, so the threshold current I<sub>th</sub> falls further.

quiz.q: A laser has I<sub>th</sub> = 25 mA and η<sub>s</sub> = 0.25 W/A. Find the output at 55 mA.
A cavity is 300 µm long with group index 3.5, emitting at 1.3 µm. Find the longitudinal mode spacing.
A laser's threshold current doubles when the temperature rises by 30 K. Find its characteristic temperature.
quiz.a: I<sub>th</sub>(T)/I<sub>th</sub>(T₀) = exp(ΔT/T<sub>c</sub>) = 2, so T<sub>c</sub> = 30/ln 2 = 43.3 K. Such a low T<sub>c</sub> means heavy temperature dependence and a need for cooling or bias tracking.

quiz.q: Why does direct modulation of a laser add dispersion penalty in a long link?
quiz.a: Modulating the current changes the carrier density, which changes the refractive index and so the emitted wavelength during each pulse (chirp). The chirped pulse has a wider spectrum; in the fiber its wavelengths travel at different speeds, the pulse spreads, and the receiver sees intersymbol interference.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production 1.55 µm transmitters replace the plain Fabry–Perot cavity with a distributed feedback (DFB) grating that selects one longitudinal mode, or use a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL) for short data-centre links. Tunable lasers slide the grating electrically across the C-band for reconfigurable WDM networks (see WDM concepts and components). Silicon photonics puts lasers, modulators and waveguides on one chip. Search for 'DFB laser side-mode suppression ratio', 'VCSEL data link' and 'C-band tunable laser'.
